summary: This standards-track document describes PROBE, an extended form of ICMP echo used as a network diagnostic tool. Like PING, it can ask about the status of an interface. Unlike PING, it does not require two-way connectivity between the probing interface and the probed one, so it can query interfaces that are not directly reachable by the sender in the usual way.

plainLanguage.summary: Ping is like knocking on a door and waiting for an answer. PROBE lets you ask a neighbor whether a different door is open, even if you cannot knock there yourself.

questions: what is the probe diagnostic utility
how is probe different from ping
subtitle: A ping-like probe that asks a nearby proxy whether another interface is up, with no direct path to it needed.

tldr.problem: PING needs two-way connectivity between the probing and probed interfaces, so it cannot check interfaces that are unnumbered, unreachable, or on the other IP version.
tldr.mechanism: PROBE sends an ICMP Extended Echo Request to a proxy interface. The request names the probed interface in an Interface Identification Object, and the proxy answers with an Extended Echo Reply describing the interface's status.
tldr.outcome: Operators can check an interface they cannot ping directly, but nodes only answer if an operator has explicitly enabled and authorized the feature, because the data could help an attacker.

today: RFC 8335 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2018. It updates RFC 4884 by adding the Extended Echo Request and Reply to the list of extensible ICMP messages, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PING Is Not Always Enough
sections.content:
Network operators use PING to test two-way connectivity between a probing interface and a probed interface. PING sends an ICMP Echo Request and, if an Echo Reply comes back, it has verified four things: the probing node can reach the probed interface, the probed interface is active, the probed node can reach the probing interface, and the probing interface is active.

PROBE still asks about the status of an interface, but it does not need connectivity between the probing and probed interfaces. It needs two-way connectivity between the probing interface and a proxy interface. The proxy can sit on the same node as the probed interface, or on a node the probed interface is directly connected to.

The RFC lists cases where PROBE works and PING does not, assuming the probing and proxy interfaces can talk to each other:

  • the probed interface is unnumbered;
  • the probed interface has only an IPv6 link-local address and is not directly connected to the probing interface;
  • the probing interface runs IPv4 only while the probed interface runs IPv6 only, or the other way around;
  • the probing node has no route to the probed interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you cannot reach a friend's house to ask if they are home. PROBE lets you ask a neighbor who can see their house to check for you.

sections.title: The Five Roles
sections.content:
The RFC names the interfaces and nodes involved. The probing interface sends the ICMP Extended Echo Request, and the probing node is where it lives. The proxy interface receives the request, and the proxy node is where it lives. The probed interface is the one whose status is being asked about, and the probed node is where that interface lives.

If the proxy and probed interfaces are on the same node, the proxy node is also the probed node. Otherwise the proxy node is directly connected to the probed node.

How the proxy finds the answer depends on that. For a probed interface on the proxy node, PROBE reports status the way it would determine an oper-status: if oper-status is 'up' (1), the interface is reported active, otherwise inactive. For a probed interface on a directly connected node, PROBE looks in the IPv4 ARP table or IPv6 Neighbor Cache and reports reachability if the interface appears there, or reports that the table entry does not exist.
sections.plainLanguage: There is the person asking, the neighbor who is asked, and the door being checked. The neighbor either looks at their own door or peeks at the one next to theirs.

sections.title: The ICMP Extended Echo Request
sections.content:
The Extended Echo Request exists for both ICMPv4 (Type 42) and ICMPv6 (Type 160). It is carried in an ordinary IPv4 or IPv6 header whose Source Address is the probing interface and whose Destination Address is the proxy interface; both must be unicast.

Code MUST be 0 and is ignored on receipt. Identifier and Sequence Number help match replies to requests and may be 0. The Reserved field MUST be 0. The L (local) bit is set if the probed interface lives on the proxy node and clear if it is directly connected to the proxy node.

After the fixed part comes an ICMP Extension Structure as defined in RFC 4884. It MUST contain exactly one Interface Identification Object. With the L-bit set, the object may name the probed interface by name, index or address. With the L-bit clear, it MUST use an address. An address can be from any address family, so even an ICMPv4 request can ask about an IPv6 or IEEE 802 address.
sections.plainLanguage: The request is a note to the neighbor. It says whether to check their own door or the next one over, and it names the door.

sections.title: The Interface Identification Object
sections.content:
This object tells the proxy which interface is meant. Its header holds Class-Num (value 3), a C-Type and a Length in octets that covers the header and payload. The C-Type says how the interface is identified: 1 by name, 2 by index, 3 by address.

By name, the payload is the interface name as defined in RFC 7223, padded with ASCII NULL characters to a 32-bit boundary if needed. By index, the length is 8 and the payload holds the if-index from RFC 7223.

By address (C-Type 3), the payload has a 16-bit Address Family Identifier (AFI), an Address Length, a Reserved byte set to 0, and then the address, padded with zeroes to a 32-bit boundary. Any value in the IANA Address Family Numbers registry is valid as an AFI.
sections.plainLanguage: The object is the name tag on the door you are asking about. It can be the door's name, its number, or its street address.

sections.title: The ICMP Extended Echo Reply
sections.content:
The reply uses Type 43 for ICMPv4 and Type 161 for ICMPv6. Its IP addresses are swapped from the request, and its Identifier and Sequence Number are copied so the prober can match it up.

The Code field says whether the query worked: 0 No Error, 1 Malformed Query, 2 No Such Interface, 3 No Such Table Entry, 4 Multiple Interfaces Satisfy Query.

The State field is 0 unless Code is 0 and the probed interface is on a directly connected node. In that case it mirrors the ARP or Neighbor Cache entry: 1 Incomplete, 2 Reachable, 3 Stale, 4 Delay, 5 Probe, 6 Failed (0 is Reserved). Three flag bits report on a local probed interface: A is set when Code is 0, the interface is on the proxy node and it is active; the 4 and 6 bits are set, only if A is set, when IPv4 or IPv6 is running on that interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The neighbor writes back a short answer: the door is open, it is closed, or I could not find it. For a door next to theirs they also say how recently they saw someone there.

sections.title: How a Node Handles a Request
sections.content:
A node MUST silently discard an Extended Echo Request, with no reply at all, if any of these is true: it does not recognize the message; it has not explicitly enabled the feature; the Source Address is not authorized for that L-bit setting or for that query type (by name, index or address); the Source Address is not a unicast address; or the Destination Address is a multicast address.

Otherwise the node builds a reply. For ICMPv4 it sets the Don't Fragment flag to 1, More Fragments to 0, Fragment Offset to 0, TTL to 255 and the protocol to ICMP. For ICMPv6 it sets Hop Limit to 255 and Next Header to ICMPv6. In both cases it swaps the addresses, sets the DiffServ codepoint to CS0, copies Identifier and Sequence Number, sets the Code, sets the checksum and forwards the reply.

The flag bits and State are filled in as described for the reply. With the L-bit set, a Code of 0 and an active interface, the A bit and the 4 and 6 bits are set as appropriate. With the L-bit clear and a Code of 0, State reflects the ARP or Neighbor Cache entry.
sections.plainLanguage: The neighbor only answers if you were told you may ask. If they are not allowed to answer you, they say nothing at all.

sections.title: Choosing the Reply Code
sections.content:
The Code is 1 Malformed Query if the request has no ICMP Extension Structure, does not have exactly one Interface Identification Object, has the L-bit clear while naming the interface by name or index, or is otherwise malformed.

It is 2 No Such Interface if the L-bit is set and the named interface is not on the proxy node. It is 3 No Such Table Entry if the L-bit is clear and the address is not in the ARP table or IPv6 Neighbor Cache. It is 4 Multiple Interfaces Satisfy Query if the L-bit is set and more than one interface on the proxy node matches, or the L-bit is clear and the address maps to multiple table entries. Otherwise the Code is 0 No Error.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer comes with a reason when something goes wrong: the question was confusing, there is no such door, or there are several doors that match.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PROBE has legitimate uses, such as finding an interface's operational status or which protocols (IPv4 or IPv6) are active on it. A malicious party could also use it to discover interface names, and from a name might infer the interface bandwidth, the type of device (such as the vendor) and the operating system version it runs.

So nodes that support the feature MUST offer these configuration options: enable or disable the feature (disabled by default); which L-bit settings are enabled (by default setting the L-bit is enabled and clearing it is disabled); which query types are enabled (all disabled by default); the prefixes allowed to send each enabled query type; and, for each interface, whether requests are accepted. A request the node is not configured to support MUST be silently discarded.

PROBE must not leak information about one VPN into another. If the proxy interface is in a different VPN than the probed interface, the node MUST reply with code 2, No Such Interface. Implementations SHOULD rate-limit incoming requests to protect local resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the neighbor could tell strangers too much about your house, the feature starts switched off. A grown-up has to say who may ask and what they may ask.

messages.label: Extended Echo Request
messages.note: Carries an Interface Identification Object naming the probed interface.

messages.label: Extended Echo Reply
messages.note: Reports the status of the probed interface, if access is granted.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Set to 0 and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Helps match replies to requests; may be 0.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Helps match replies to requests; may be 0.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Set if the probed interface is on the proxy node.

fields.name: State
fields.desc: ARP or Neighbor Cache entry state.

fields.name: Res
fields.desc: Set to 0 and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Active: probed interface on the proxy node is active.

items.label: Malformed Query
items.desc: The request was missing or had a bad extension or object.

items.label: No Such Interface
items.desc: The L-bit was set and no such interface is on the proxy node.

items.label: No Such Table Entry
items.desc: The L-bit was clear and the address is not in the ARP table or Neighbor Cache.

items.label: Multiple Interfaces Satisfy Query
items.desc: More than one interface or table entry matches.
